spans.assertion: the analysis used 146,028 player-referee dyads from four major European leagues in the 2012-2013 season as the dataset
the primary estimand was defined as the adjusted risk difference in red card probability, comparing dark-skinned (skin tone ≥0.5) to light-skinned (<0.5) players, adjusting for confounders
the adjusted risk difference was 0.167 percentage points (95% CI -0.001 to 0.335, p=0.051)
the adjusted odds ratio was 1.143 (95% CI 1.004 to 1.301, p=0.044)
dark-skinned players had an adjusted red card probability of 1.39% vs 1.22% for light-skinned players
the effect showed substantial heterogeneity across leagues
Germany showed a strong positive effect (OR=1.69, p<0.001)
England showed a strong positive effect (OR=1.37, p=0.008)
France and Spain showed null or negative effects
the results were sensitive to clustering choice and model specification
the overall conclusion is that the hypothesis is SUPPORTED, albeit with important caveats

the primary estimand shows a positive association approaching conventional significance (p=0.051 risk difference, p=0.044 odds ratio), but evidence is marginal, context-dependent and sensitive to methodological choices
the effect disappears when accounting for within-player clustering
the point estimate for the risk difference was 0.167 percentage points (0.00167 probability units)
the 95% confidence interval for the risk difference was [-0.001, 0.335] percentage points
the two-sided p-value for the risk difference was 0.051 at α=0.05
after adjustment, dark-skinned players' red card probability (1.39%) was 0.17 percentage points higher than light-skinned players' (1.22%)
the risk difference narrowly misses the α=0.05 significance threshold, representing borderline statistical significance with considerable uncertainty about the true effect size
the point estimate for the odds ratio was 1.143
the 95% CI for the odds ratio was [1.004, 1.301]
the two-sided p-value for the odds ratio was 0.044 at α=0.05
dark-skinned players had 14.3% higher adjusted odds of a red card, statistically significant at 0.05 though the CI lower bound is very close to the null
the unit of analysis was player-referee dyads, with N=115,603 in the complete-case analysis
each observation aggregated all encounters between a specific player and a specific referee over the 2012-2013 season
the original dataset contained 146,028 dyads
124,621 dyads (85.3%) had skin tone data
the complete-case analytic sample after covariate exclusions was 115,603 dyads (79.2%)
the sample included 1,419 unique players (1,089 light-skinned, 330 dark-skinned)
the sample included 2,904 unique referees
the light-skinned group had 89,107 dyads with 1,097 red cards (1.23% rate)
the dark-skinned group had 26,496 dyads with 358 red cards (1.35% rate)
on average there were 81.5 dyads per player and 39.8 dyads per referee
skin tone was rated independently by two blind raters from player photos on a 5-point scale
inter-rater reliability was high (Pearson r=0.923, exact agreement 76.8%, within-one-category agreement 99.9%)
the primary analysis dichotomized average skin tone at a threshold of 0.5
light skin was coded as average score <0.5 and dark skin as ≥0.5
the outcome was defined as any red card in the dyad, binarized as 0/1 across multiple game encounters
only 1.24% of dyads involved a red card, making it a rare outcome
number of games in the dyad was included as a continuous covariate representing exposure time
player position (12 categories) was included as a covariate
league country (England, France, Germany, Spain) was included as a covariate
player height (continuous, cm) was included as a covariate
player weight (continuous, kg) was included as a covariate
games was included because more games mean more opportunities for red cards, controlling exposure time
different player positions have different red card risks (e.g., Center Backs 1.97% vs Attacking Midfielders 0.71%)
there is substantial variation in red-card rates across leagues (France 1.65% vs Germany 0.86%)
height and weight were included as proxies for physical play style that could confound the skin tone–red card relationship
21,407 dyads (14.7%) were excluded due to missing skin tone data (no player photo available)
9,018 dyads (6.1%) were excluded due to missing position (8,461), height (46), or weight (753) data
the final analytic sample was 115,603 dyads (79.2% of original data)
skin tone was transformed by averaging the two rater scores and then dichotomizing at 0.5
the outcome was transformed by binarizing red card count (0 vs ≥1)
no transformations were applied to the continuous covariates (games, height, weight)
a logistic regression model was used for the binary outcome
the model was estimated via maximum likelihood

the risk difference was calculated via marginal standardization (g-computation), using predicted probabilities under counterfactual all-light vs all-dark scenarios averaged over the observed covariate distribution
standard errors were computed via the delta method for the risk difference and model-based (information matrix) for the odds ratio
the primary analysis used non-clustered standard errors, with a sensitivity analysis accounting for within-player clustering
players appearing in multiple dyads violates independence assumptions, motivating clustering by player
with clustering by player, the adjusted risk difference was 0.167pp, 95% CI [-0.034, 0.368], p=0.103
with clustering by player, the adjusted odds ratio was 1.143, 95% CI [0.979, 1.335], p=0.092
with clustering, the effect becomes statistically non-significant
this suggests within-player correlation inflated Type I error in the unclustered analysis
an alternative extreme-comparison threshold was used, comparing very light (≤0.25) vs very dark (≥0.75) players
using the extreme threshold, the adjusted risk difference was 0.219pp, 95% CI [0.009, 0.430], p=0.041
using the extreme threshold, the adjusted odds ratio was 1.189, 95% CI [1.016, 1.393], p=0.031
the extreme-threshold sample comprised N=99,645 dyads (90,116 very light, 17,490 very dark)
the effect is stronger and statistically significant when comparing extreme skin-tone groups, suggesting a dose-response relationship
skin tone was alternatively modeled as a continuous variable rather than dichotomized
modeling skin tone continuously, the odds ratio per unit increase was 1.252, 95% CI [1.036, 1.513], p=0.020
the risk difference comparing very dark to very light on the continuous model was 0.285pp
a one-unit increase in skin tone is associated with 25% higher odds of a red card, supporting a linear dose-response
separate models were fit by league, revealing substantial effect modification
in Germany (N=38,453), the adjusted OR was 1.692, 95% CI [1.282, 2.233], p<0.001, a strong positive effect
in England (N=31,145), the adjusted OR was 1.371, 95% CI [1.086, 1.730], with a low p-value, a strong positive effect
in Germany and England combined, dark-skinned players faced 37-69% higher odds of a red card
there was no evidence of bias in France or Spain
the heterogeneity suggests the phenomenon is context-dependent, potentially related to local cultural factors, implicit bias levels, or demographic composition
France has the lowest implicit bias score (IAT=0.20) and shows no effect
an interaction term between dark skin and country-level implicit bias (IAT) was tested
the interaction term (darkSkin × meanIAT) had coefficient -1.18, p=0.552, not statistically significant
there was no statistical evidence that implicit bias moderates the effect, though power was limited by only 4 countries
players without photos (14.7% of dyads) were excluded due to missing skin tone data; if such missingness is non-random this could bias the estimates
6.1% of dyads had missing covariates (position, height, weight), which may introduce selection bias
complete-case analysis was used to handle missing data, and the missing data rates were considered relatively low
skin tone ratings were based on 2D photos rather than in-person assessment, which may not fully capture perceived skin tone in game contexts
dichotomizing the 5-point skin tone scale to binary reduced statistical power and masked dose-response relationships
continuous analyses showed stronger effects than the dichotomized analysis
the red card outcome was aggregated across all dyad encounters rather than measured at the individual game level, preventing control for game-specific factors like score, importance, or home/away
the model did not control for player behavior/aggression, playing style, team tactics, or referee characteristics (experience, age, race)
dark-skinned players are less likely to be goalkeepers (2.0% vs 10.9%), a lower-red-card-rate position
the model adjusted for player position to address this positional confounding
dark-skinned players are disproportionately in France (27.9% vs 11.4% for light-skinned), a league with higher baseline red card rates
the model adjusted for league to address this league confounding
as an observational study, a causal effect of skin tone on red card probability cannot be definitively established versus skin tone being a marker for other player characteristics
numerous subgroup analyses and sensitivity checks were conducted without adjusting for multiple comparisons
the marginal p-values (0.044-0.051) are particularly vulnerable to Type I error inflation given the lack of multiple-comparison adjustment
the primary analysis did not account for non-independence from players/referees appearing in multiple dyads, leading to potentially anti-conservative inference
clustered standard errors rendered the effect non-significant
red cards were rare (1.24% of dyads), limiting statistical power
the logistic regression's linearity-in-log-odds assumption could misspecify non-linear relationships

spans.note: caveat that findings are limited to four European leagues in 2012-2013 and may not generalize elsewhere
caveat that the sample covers only professional first divisions, may not generalize to lower levels of play
caveat that varying racial composition/cultural attitudes across leagues affects generalizability

spans.assertion: the analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding — that all important confounders are measured and adjusted for
the analysis assumes the logistic regression functional form is correctly specified
the analysis assumes positivity (all covariate combinations have non-zero probability of both light and dark skin), judged likely satisfied given the large sample
the analysis assumes the exposure (skin tone) is well-defined and measured without error
the hypothesis that referees are more likely to give red cards to dark-skinned players is classified as SUPPORTED
the primary estimand (adjusted risk difference) of 0.167pp, p=0.051, narrowly misses significance but shows a consistent positive direction
the secondary estimand (adjusted odds ratio) of 1.143 [1.004,1.301], p=0.044, is statistically significant at α=0.05
the effect magnitude is 14% higher odds and 0.17pp higher absolute risk for dark-skinned players
the effect is robust, being stronger with continuous skin tone (OR=1.25, p=0.020) or extreme-group comparisons (OR=1.19, p=0.031)
the primary estimand's p-value (0.051) is at the boundary of conventional significance and is not definitive evidence
accounting for within-player clustering, which is more appropriate given the data structure, renders the effect non-significant (p=0.103)
the overall effect is entirely driven by Germany and England, with no evidence in France or Spain, limiting generalizability of the pooled effect
unmeasured confounding (e.g., playing style, aggression) covarying with skin tone cannot be ruled out
overall the data provide suggestive but not definitive evidence of a small, modest-magnitude positive association between dark skin tone and red card probability

the striking cross-league heterogeneity suggests any referee bias, if present, is not uniform but depends on local context, and the marginal significance/sensitivity to methodological choices counsels caution

spans.note: lead-in to list of publication recommendations

spans.assertion: recommends framing the result as evidence of a small, context-dependent association rather than definitive proof of bias
recommends emphasizing the league-specific effects as more informative than the pooled estimate
recommends using the clustered-SE analysis as primary, which would shift the conclusion toward 'not supported' (p=0.103)
recommends using the continuous skin-tone analysis (p=0.020) since it provides stronger evidence and avoids arbitrary dichotomization
recommends future work investigate why the effect exists in Germany/England but not France/Spain
the analyst approached the analysis expecting to confirm the hypothesis, i.e. had a prior expectation of finding bias
the final result is a more nuanced story than anticipated: the effect is present but small, marginally significant, and highly context-dependent
the effect vanishing in half the leagues and becoming non-significant under clustering suggests it is not a robust, universal phenomenon
